# RYAN (Ryan Specialty Holdings, Inc.) — Value Investor Note

## Circle of Competence
Understandable at the business-model level: Ryan Specialty is a wholesale insurance broker / managing general underwriter (MGU) that sits between retail insurance brokers and carriers, specializing in placing complex, hard-to-fit excess & surplus (E&S) risk that doesn't fit standard-market underwriting. It earns commissions and fees, not underwriting risk itself - asset-light, no balance-sheet insurance liability exposure. The part requiring real judgment, not certainty, is how much of its current earnings power is durable operating economics versus a GAAP presentation still working through IPO-era accounting noise (see Predictability below).

## Moat & Durability — Score 7/10
The moat rests on three legs: (1) underwriting/placement expertise and delegated binding authority that let it profitably underwrite risk classes generalist brokers can't easily touch, (2) scale and carrier relationships built over years that are slow for a new entrant to replicate, and (3) switching costs - once a retail broker routes a class of complex business through a wholesale partner, re-routing it elsewhere is operationally disruptive. There's a genuine secular tailwind too: growing complexity and severity of risk (cyber, climate, casualty) keeps pushing more premium out of the standard market and into E&S, which is Ryan's home turf. The moat is narrower than a brand-name retail broker's, though - Ryan has no pricing power over the carriers whose paper it places, and its revenue is fundamentally geared to the insurance underwriting cycle. A meaningfully softening market (more capacity, falling rates) compresses commission growth industry-wide, moat or no moat. Real, but cyclical rather than bulletproof - hence 7, not 9.

## Management & Capital Allocation
What the numbers say: 22.1% ROE and a 25% operating margin point to an efficiently-run core distribution business. But debt/equity of 374.7% (debt at roughly 3.75x book equity) means a real chunk of that ROE is leverage amplification, not pure operating alpha - lever any decent business 3-4x and ROE looks better than the underlying economics alone would produce. FCF yield of only 3.58% is a further tell: cash conversion is respectable, not exceptional, for a model that's supposed to be asset-light. This packet has no visibility into buyback pace, dividend policy, insider ownership, or M&A discipline (wholesale brokers commonly grow via bolt-on acquisitions of smaller MGAs/binding facilities) - all of that has to be taken on faith rather than verified from what's here. Trustworthy-management is a reasonable working assumption given the operating margins, but the heavy leverage means capital allocation quality matters more here than in a lower-debt peer, and that's precisely the part we can't audit from this packet.

## Predictability
The standout data point is the gap between trailing P/E (56.6x) and forward P/E (17.4x) - a roughly 3x difference in implied earnings power. That kind of gap is common in recently-public, Up-C-structured specialty insurers carrying tax-receivable-agreement remeasurements or founder/pre-IPO equity-comp charges that hit GAAP earnings without being ongoing cash costs - but this packet gives no line-item way to confirm that read versus the less comfortable alternative, that trailing earnings reflect real recurring costs the forward estimate is optimistically assuming away. Revenue growth of 7.4% is solid but unspectacular for the multiple being paid on a forward basis. Momentum adds to the uncertainty rather than resolving it: -27.4% over twelve months, then +34.6% over the last three, with price now sitting almost exactly on the 200-day moving average (-0.34%) - a market that has been repricing this story hard in both directions, not calmly compounding it. This fails Munger's 'easy decision' test even though the underlying distribution business is simple to describe.

## Inversion — How an Owner Loses Money From Here
1. **Cycle turns while leverage is high**: the E&S market softens (more capacity, falling rates), organic commission growth slows well below 7.4%, and 3.75x debt/equity leaves little cushion to absorb the downturn - equity value is the leveraged residual, so a modest EBITDA decline could produce an outsized equity-value decline.
2. **The P/E gap is real, not one-time**: if trailing GAAP earnings (implying the 56.6x multiple) turn out to reflect recurring economic costs - financing expense on the debt load, dilutive equity comp, ongoing TRA payments - rather than a one-off item, then normalized owner earnings look a lot closer to the depressed trailing run-rate than to the rosier forward estimate, and the stock is far more expensive than the forward P/E suggests.
3. **Roll-up execution risk**: wholesale brokers typically grow partly through bolt-on M&A; overpaying for tuck-ins or failing to integrate them compounds balance-sheet risk on an already highly-levered structure. Notably, 12.5% of float is sold short with 5.96 days to cover - a real, sized bear thesis is already positioned against this name, not just noise.

## Valuation
The packet does not include share price or share count, so per-share figures require a disclosed modeling assumption. Using an approximate ~275M diluted share count (not sourced from the packet - a rough estimate consistent with the reported $16.33B market cap producing a plausible current price) implies a current price near **$59.4/share**, trailing EPS near $1.05, forward EPS near $3.42, and FCF/share near $2.13.

Given the trailing/forward EPS split flagged above, I don't trust either figure alone as owner earnings. Blending FCF/share ($2.13, the more cash-grounded number) with a haircut on the optimistic forward EPS (~$3.42 × 0.85 to discount for SBC add-backs and estimate optimism, ≈ $2.91) gives a normalized owner-earnings estimate of roughly **$2.50-2.55/share**.

Applying a quality-adjusted multiple range that reflects real moat and 20%+ ROE on one hand, and real cyclicality plus 3.75x leverage risk on the other:
- **Low case** (15x owner earnings, reflecting leverage/cycle risk): ~$40/share
- **High case** (21x owner earnings, if the trailing-P/E depression proves genuinely one-time and growth holds near 7-8%): ~$55/share

Midpoint ~$47.5/share vs. an implied current price of ~$59.4/share gives a **negative margin of safety of roughly -25%** - the stock screens as paying up relative to a conservative owner-earnings read, even though the more favorable EV/EBITDA multiple (10.25x, reasonable-to-cheap for a specialty distributor by broker-industry standards) argues the market isn't pricing this as an obviously expensive name. That tension - cheap on EV/EBITDA, rich on a normalized-owner-earnings basis - is exactly why this is a 'watch,' not a clean pass or buy.

## The Cloning Caveat
Vulcan Value Partners (VVP), a concentrated value manager, added in both Q1 2026 (+42.7% shares, landing at 1.77% of portfolio) and Q2 2026 (+19.97% shares, landing at 1.51% of portfolio) - two consecutive quarters of buying is a real signal of sustained conviction, not a one-off. Worth noting, though: the position's *share of portfolio* actually declined quarter-over-quarter (1.77% → 1.51%) even as share count rose, so this reads as steady accumulation rather than escalating high-conviction sizing - for a concentrated manager, sub-2% positions are still a moderate, not maximal, bet. Torray Funds' Q2 2026 add lands at just 0.06% of portfolio - immaterial, basket exposure only, not a signal worth weighting. Net: real value-investor interest exists here, which corroborates that the business has some merit, but nobody shown in this packet is betting big on it - this is supporting evidence for doing the work, not a substitute for an independent valuation call.

## Verdict
**Watch, conviction 5/10.** An understandable, moderately moated specialty-insurance distribution business with good operating margins and ROE, but the ROE leans on heavy leverage (3.75x debt/equity), earnings predictability is clouded by a large trailing-vs-forward P/E gap this packet can't resolve, and a conservative owner-earnings estimate implies the current price is roughly 25% above fair value. The corroborating superinvestor buying (Vulcan Value Partners, moderate and steady rather than maximal) supports keeping this on the watch list for a better entry point or clearer visibility into which of the trailing/forward earnings figures is closer to the truth - it does not yet clear the bar for a buy at Munger-strict standards.
momentum_thesis: RYAN is mid-reversal, not mid-trend: the 12-month tape is still down 27.4% and 6-month is a further -4.8%, but the last quarter ripped +34.6% and the last month added another +3.0%, dragging price back to essentially flat versus the 200DMA (-0.34%) with RSI14 at a neutral 58.9 — room to run before overbought, no immediate exhaustion signal. Positioning has flipped constructive into this move: short interest is a meaningful 12.5% of float at 5.96 days to cover, and the options market is aggressively call-skewed (put/call OI of 0.15), a combination that reads as shorts leaning against a base that's now breaking their way rather than a crowded long. Superinvestor flow corroborates the turn rather than chasing it — Vulcan Value Partners built the position across two straight quarters (+42.7% shares in Q1 2026, +20.0% more in Q2 2026, now ~1.5-1.8% of its book), a value shop's conviction accumulation through the drawdown, not a momentum tourist buying the bounce. Torray's Q2 add is a rounding-error stake (0.06% of portfolio) and carries little signal. Net: this looks like early-innings squeeze-and-reversal off a beaten-down base with real sponsorship underneath it, but the stock still has to prove it can clear the 200DMA rather than stall at it. High leverage (debt/equity 374.7%) means the underlying business has limited margin for error if the setup fails.
